domain_label: TOEFL iBT (2026 format) — Section-Skills Syllabus: question type -> underlying skill -> practice form
purpose: A method for turning the TOEFL iBT question line-up into a teachable syllabus: mapping every current 2026 question type (Reading: Complete the Words / Read in Daily Life / Read an Academic Passage; Listening: Listen and Choose a Response / Daily Life Conversation / Daily Life Announcement / Academic Talk; Speaking: Listen and Repeat + Take an Interview; Writing: Build a Sentence + Write an Email + Writing for an Academic Discussion) to the underlying language skill it measures and a concrete practice form a from-zero learner can drill, keeping the legacy 2023-2025 task types mapped where published prep material still uses them, and tagging every claim FACT / ESTIMATE / UNKNOWN exactly as the grounding research file did (ETS pages were unreachable from the research sandbox, so all ETS-page claims are search-excerpt-verified, and third-party item counts, timings and 2026 rubric dimensions are estimates, never invented as fact).
assumptions: no observed learner dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

the current test is the January 21, 2026 overhaul (four sections, ~2 hours, Reading/Listening two-stage adaptive, 1-6 band scoring) per ETS press release and update pages verified via search excerpts; the 2023-2025 legacy format is carried only because most published prep material still describes it

the per-section item counts, timings and exact 2026 Speaking/Writing rubric dimensions are third-party or search-excerpt estimates because the ETS Blueprint PDF and rubric PDFs were not fetchable from the research sandbox; they are used as planning priors and tagged, never quoted as ETS-confirmed fact
the exact on-test section order and the full CEFR-to-band cell table are UNKNOWN (sources conflict / ETS table not fetchable) and are represented as named blockers, not invented
exclusions: the whole-test structure, timing budget, scoring scale mechanics, registration, delivery modes and retake policy (those are the exam-structure KB kb_exam_structure in this same specialist)
band-target study-hour prescriptions and a full week-by-week study calendar (no ETS hour guidance exists; the research file flags it UNKNOWN)
quoting exact fees, exact adaptive item counts, exact rubric weightings, or CEFR-to-band cutoff cells as fact — all UNKNOWN or estimate in the research file
reviewing or ranking specific third-party practice vendors beyond naming that official ETS TestReady and the free sample test are the authoritative practice spine

competency_questions.question: How does this KB turn a TOEFL question type into a teachable unit — what is the question-type -> underlying-skill -> practice-form mapping method?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SECTION_SKILL_FRAME states that each 2026 question type is decomposed into the single language skill it measures and a concrete drillable practice form, and that this triple is the unit of expert work the whole syllabus is built from

competency_questions.question: Which task types are current 2026 and which are legacy 2023-2025, and how is legacy prep material mapped without misleading a learner?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FORMAT_ERA_SPLIT dates the Jan 21 2026 overhaul and lists what changed, and LEGACY_TASK_MAP maps the retired legacy tasks (4-task Speaking, 2-passage Reading, Integrated+WAD Writing) to the current skills so old prep is reusable but not mistaken for the current line-up

competency_questions.question: What does the two-stage adaptive model mean for Reading and Listening, and what skill does it add on top of the item skills?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ADAPTIVE_STAGE_MODEL states Reading and Listening are two-stage (everyone gets Stage 1; Stage 2 difficulty/count/time adjust to Stage 1 performance), names pacing-under-adaptive-difficulty as the added skill, and tags the exact per-module item counts as third-party estimates

competency_questions.question: What skill does Complete the Words measure and what is a from-zero practice form for it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: R_COMPLETE_THE_WORDS describes the ~70-100 word paragraph with 10 second-half-deleted words and intact first sentence, names vocabulary + orthographic/lexical processing as the skill, and prescribes a form-completion-from-context drill fed by the high-frequency vocabulary base

competency_questions.question: What skill does Read in Daily Life measure and how is it practised?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: R_DAILY_LIFE describes the ~15-150 word practical texts (emails, texts, menus, bills, announcements) with multiple choice, names everyday functional-English comprehension across the A1-C2 range as the skill, and gives a scan-a-practical-text-for-the-asked-fact drill

competency_questions.question: What skill does Read an Academic Passage measure and how does its ~200-word 2026 form change practice versus the ~700-word legacy passage?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: R_ACADEMIC_PASSAGE names academic reading for main idea/detail/inference/vocabulary-in-context, states the ~200-word passage + ~5 MC (vs ~700 legacy), notes no prior knowledge is needed, and gives a short-passage question-type drill

competency_questions.question: How do the four 2026 Listening task types map to distinct listening sub-skills and practice forms?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: the four Listening nodes separate pragmatic response selection (L1), conversation comprehension with facts-vs-opinion (L2), key-info extraction from an announcement (L3) and academic listening for main idea/detail/purpose (L4), each with a practice form, and flag that per-type item counts vary by adaptive module (estimate)

competency_questions.question: What do the two 2026 Speaking tasks measure and how are they practised, given Listen and Repeat is exact repetition and Take an Interview has no prep time?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: S_LISTEN_REPEAT states 7 sentences heard once and repeated aloud, measuring phonological/oral fluency, intelligibility and exact repetition accuracy; S_TAKE_INTERVIEW states 4 escalating questions at 45s each with no prep, measuring spontaneous language use, organization, fluency and coherence, each with a drill

competency_questions.question: What do the three 2026 Writing tasks measure and how does each get its own practice form?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: W_BUILD_SENTENCE names syntax/word-order control (a sentence-assembly drill), W_EMAIL names practical written communication and register in a 7-minute scenario email, and W_ACADEMIC_DISCUSSION names reasoned argument in a 10-minute discussion-board post (carried from July 2023), each with a distinct drill

competency_questions.question: How do the CEFR difficulty ladder and vocabulary-size targets sit under the tasks and decide which task a from-zero learner drills first?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CEFR_DIFFICULTY_LADDER places the tasks on the A1-C2 spread (R1/S1 reach down to A1; R2/L2/L3/W2 are everyday A2-B1; academic items reach C1/C2) and VOCAB_FOUNDATION carries the Milton & Alexiou lexical-size anchors (A2 ~1500-2500, B1 ~2750-3250, B2 ~3250-3750 [FACT]) with the ~8000-9000 word-family academic figure flagged estimate and not required for band 4

competency_questions.question: How is practice for the productive Speaking/Writing tasks aligned to the scoring rubrics without over-claiming the exact 2026 rubric dimensions?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RUBRIC_ALIGNED_PRACTICE ties each productive task to its rubric focus (legacy Speaking dimensions Delivery/Language Use/Topic Development [FACT]; 2026 Listen-and-Repeat fluency/intelligibility/repeat-accuracy and Writing elaboration/syntax/conventions [ESTIMATE]) and names the exact 2026 dimension weightings as an UNKNOWN blocker not to be quoted

competency_questions.question: How is a practice form designed per question type, which underlying skills transfer across tasks, and what is the composed section-skills syllabus?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRACTICE_FORM_DESIGN states how a drillable form is built for a type, SKILL_TRANSFER_MAP shows shared skills (phonics/high-frequency vocab under R1+S1; functional comprehension under R2+L2/L3), and SECTION_SKILL_SYLLABUS composes the full type->skill->form syllabus with the section-order UNKNOWN flagged

glossary.definition: The core method of this KB: decompose each TOEFL question type into (1) the single underlying language skill it measures and (2) a concrete practice form a learner can drill, so a syllabus is a table of type -> skill -> form rather than a list of task names.

The current test is the January 21, 2026 overhaul (four sections, ~2 hours, Reading/Listening two-stage adaptive, 1-6 CEFR-aligned band scoring, scores within 72 hours) per ETS press release/update pages [FACT via search excerpts]; the legacy format is the July 26, 2023 - January 20, 2026 test (2-passage Reading, 28-question Listening, 4-task Speaking, Integrated + Academic Discussion Writing) still described by most published prep material.

Reading and Listening are multistage adaptive: every test taker gets the same Stage 1, and Stage 2 difficulty, item count and time adjust to Stage 1 performance [FACT]; exact per-module item counts (~up to 50 Reading / ~47 Listening items, 35 raw points each) are third-party blueprint estimates, not ETS-confirmed here.

A 2026 Reading task: a ~70-100 word paragraph in which 10 words have their second half deleted and must be typed in, with the first sentence left intact for context; it measures vocabulary knowledge plus orthographic/lexical processing (form-focused reading) [FACT for mechanics, blueprint-derived third parties].

A 2026 Reading task: short practical texts (~15-150 words) such as emails, texts, menus, bills and announcements with multiple-choice questions, measuring comprehension of everyday functional English across an A1-C2 range [FACT for mechanics].

A 2026 Speaking task: 7 sentences about campus/daily-life topics, each heard once and repeated aloud, measuring phonological/oral fluency, intelligibility and exact repetition accuracy; the 2026 scoring guide reportedly includes a descriptor like 'the response exactly repeats the prompt' [FACT existence; dimension detail ESTIMATE].

A 2026 Speaking task: a simulated interview with a prerecorded interviewer, 4 questions on one topic at 45 seconds each with no prep time, questions escalating from personal experience to broader opinion, measuring spontaneous language use, organization, fluency and coherence [FACT for mechanics].

glossary.term: Writing for an Academic Discussion (W3 / WAD)
glossary.definition: A written task carried over from the July 2023 format into 2026: the learner reads a professor's discussion-board prompt plus classmate posts and writes their own reasoned contribution in ~10 minutes, measuring relevance, elaboration, syntax and vocabulary [FACT it persists into 2026; ~10-min timing confirmed via 2026 sources].

The 2026 scoring scale: each section 1.0-6.0 in 0.5 bands, overall the four-section average rounded to the nearest half band, CEFR-labelled (A1-C2), with transitional dual reporting alongside a comparable 0-120 score through ~Jan 2028 [FACT via search excerpts]; the full CEFR-to-band cell table is UNKNOWN (ETS table not fetchable).

The concrete, repeatable drill a learner performs to build a task's skill (e.g., a context-cued word-completion drill for R1, a hear-once-repeat drill for S1, a timed 10-minute discussion-post drill for W3); the deliverable half of every section-skill mapping, anchored on the free ETS TestReady daily activity and the free Jan-2026 sample test as the authoritative spine.

nodes.definition: Establish the method the whole syllabus is built on: every TOEFL question type is decomposed into a triple — the question type as the exam faces it, the single underlying language skill it actually measures, and a concrete practice form a from-zero learner can drill repeatedly. A syllabus is then a table of these triples, not a list of task names, so study time is spent on the measured skill rather than on rehearsing the surface format. This frame is the root unit of expert work; every downstream node instantiates it for one type or one cross-cutting skill.

included: the type -> skill -> practice-form decomposition
the principle that the measured skill, not the surface format, is the study target
the frame as the reusable unit every node instantiates
excluded: the whole-test structure and scoring mechanics (exam-structure KB)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a renamed type or a too-coarse mapping changes the frame

pros.claim: Mapping to the underlying skill lets one drill serve the skill even as ETS revises the surface format
pros.example: a high-frequency-vocabulary drill feeding both Complete the Words and Listen and Repeat rather than a format-specific rehearsal

cons.claim: A skill decomposition can under-rehearse format-specific mechanics (typing missing letters, no-prep interview timing) that still cost points
cons.example: a learner strong in vocabulary who loses Complete the Words points by not practising the exact typing/interface behaviour

failure_modes: treating the task name as the study unit and drilling surface format instead of the measured skill
mapping a type to a vague skill ('reading') instead of a drillable one ('form-completion from sentence context')
acceptance_tests: the frame states the type -> skill -> practice-form triple as the unit of work and shows one worked example mapping a type to a specific skill and a specific drill
revisit_triggers: ETS revises or renames a question type
a mapping proves too coarse to yield a distinct drill
a new cross-cutting skill is identified across types

nodes.definition: Fix the era boundary that decides whether a task type is even on the test. The current test is the January 21, 2026 overhaul: four sections, ETS says to allow ~2 hours, Reading and Listening are two-stage adaptive, scoring moved to a 1-6 CEFR-aligned band scale, scores arrive within 72 hours, and content shifted toward modern daily-life English (emails, announcements, conversations) [FACT via ETS press release/update pages, verified through search excerpts because ets.org was unreachable from the research sandbox]. The legacy format (July 26, 2023 - January 20, 2026) had 2-passage Reading, 28-question Listening, a 4-task Speaking set and Integrated + Academic Discussion Writing [FACT]. Most published prep material still describes the legacy test, so a learner must know which era a resource belongs to before trusting its task list.

included: the Jan 21 2026 overhaul date and headline changes
the legacy 2023-2025 task line-up for reference
the search-excerpt honesty caveat on ETS-page claims
excluded: the detailed legacy-to-current skill mapping (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a further ETS format change or direct page access updates the split

pros.claim: Dating each format stops a learner drilling retired tasks from legacy prep material
pros.example: recognising a '4-task Speaking' guide as legacy and not budgeting time for Independent + 3 Integrated tasks that no longer exist

cons.claim: The overhaul is recent and third-party descriptions still lag, so some resources mix eras and mislead
cons.example: a 2025-dated site describing the 2026 Speaking as two tasks but keeping legacy timing tables

failure_modes: trusting a legacy resource's task list as current
mixing legacy timings/counts into the 2026 line-up
acceptance_tests: the split states the Jan 21 2026 overhaul with its headline changes and the legacy line-up, and carries the ETS-unreachable/search-excerpt honesty caveat
revisit_triggers: ETS publishes a further format change
the ETS pages become directly fetchable and confirm/correct a detail
the transition dual-reporting window ends (~Jan 2028)

nodes.definition: Model the two-stage adaptive structure that Reading and Listening now use and the skill it adds. Everyone receives the same Stage 1; Stage 2 difficulty, item count and time adjust to Stage 1 performance [FACT via ETS content-structure page, search excerpt]. On top of each item-level skill this adds pacing-under-adaptive-difficulty: because a strong Stage 1 unlocks harder, denser Stage 2 items, a learner must sustain accuracy without over-slowing. Working test time is roughly 1h23m-1h29m marketed as 'about 90 minutes'; per-module counts are widely reported as up to ~50 Reading and ~47 Listening items at 35 raw points each [ESTIMATE - medium-high, triangulated third-party blueprint readings; the ETS Blueprint PDF was not fetchable from the research sandbox]. Do not present these counts as ETS-confirmed.

included: the same-Stage-1 / adjusting-Stage-2 mechanic
pacing-under-adaptive-difficulty as the added skill
the estimate tag on per-module counts and timing

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the ETS blueprint or an adaptive-design change updates the model

pros.claim: Naming the adaptive layer makes a learner practise sustaining accuracy into a harder Stage 2, not just isolated items
pros.example: timed sets that ramp difficulty mid-set to rehearse the Stage-1-unlocks-harder-Stage-2 dynamic

cons.claim: The exact counts and per-module timing are third-party estimates, so a plan built on precise numbers can be wrong
cons.example: budgeting 'exactly 50 Reading items' from a blueprint reading the ETS PDF might not confirm

failure_modes: treating third-party item counts as the official spec
ignoring the adaptive pacing skill and practising only untimed single items
acceptance_tests: the model states the same-Stage-1 / adjusting-Stage-2 mechanic, names pacing-under-adaptive-difficulty as the added skill, and tags the item counts and timing as third-party estimates
revisit_triggers: the ETS Blueprint PDF becomes fetchable and confirms/corrects the counts
ETS changes the adaptive design
a practice-timing plan proves misaligned with the real module length

nodes.definition: Place the question types on the CEFR difficulty ladder so a from-zero learner knows which task is reachable first. The 2026 scale is CEFR-aligned by design (A1-C2), and the tasks span it: Complete the Words (R1) and Listen and Repeat (S1) reach down to A1; Read in Daily Life (R2), Daily Life Conversation (L2), Daily Life Announcement (L3) and Write an Email (W2) are everyday A2-B1 functional English; the academic Reading passage, Academic Talk and the discussion post reach into B2-C1/C2 in the upper adaptive modules [FACT that the test measures down to A1 and up to C1/C2, blueprint-derived third parties]. The ladder tells the learner to build A1-B1 functional tasks before chasing the academic ceiling; the exact CEFR-to-band cell table is UNKNOWN (the ETS table was not fetchable).

included: the A1-to-C2 placement of each task type
the build-functional-before-academic ordering for a beginner
the UNKNOWN flag on the exact CEFR-to-band cell table
excluded: the numeric band cutoffs (exam-structure KB / UNKNOWN)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an ETS CEFR table or a task-difficulty revision updates the ladder

pros.claim: Ordering tasks by CEFR level gives a beginner a defensible sequence instead of drilling the hardest task first
pros.example: starting on A1-reaching R1/S1 and A2-B1 daily-life tasks before the B2+ academic passage

cons.claim: The task-to-CEFR placement is inferred from blueprint descriptions, not a published per-item CEFR map, so the boundaries are approximate
cons.example: assuming every Read-in-Daily-Life item is A2-B1 when the range is described as A1-C2

failure_modes: sequencing a beginner straight onto the academic ceiling tasks
quoting a precise CEFR-to-band cutoff the research file marks UNKNOWN
acceptance_tests: the ladder places each task on the A1-C2 spread, prescribes functional-before-academic ordering, and flags the exact CEFR-to-band cell table as UNKNOWN
revisit_triggers: ETS publishes the full CEFR-to-band table
a task's measured difficulty range is revised
the vocabulary anchors shift the reachable-first ordering

nodes.definition: Anchor the vocabulary base the lowest tasks depend on. Milton & Alexiou (2009), a lexical-size study across 500+ learners, found A2 ~ 1,500-2,500 words, B1 ~ 2,750-3,250 and B2 ~ 3,250-3,750 (XLex-measured, first-5K band), with vocabulary size explaining ~60-70% of CEFR-level variance [FACT, citable research, not ETS]. This base directly feeds Complete the Words (form completion needs the word known) and Listen and Repeat (a known word is easier to hold and reproduce). For comfortable authentic academic reading, research after Nation commonly cites ~8,000-9,000 word families [ESTIMATE - medium], but that ceiling is NOT required for a B2/band-4 target and a beginner should not chase it early. No ETS study-hours-per-band figure exists [UNKNOWN], so no hour count is prescribed.

included: the Milton & Alexiou A2/B1/B2 lexical-size anchors as FACT
the feed into Complete the Words and Listen and Repeat
the ~8-9k word-family academic figure flagged estimate and not required for band 4

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a newer lexical-size study or a target-band change updates the anchors

pros.claim: Concrete lexical-size anchors give a beginner a measurable vocabulary target under the easiest tasks
pros.example: targeting ~2,000-2,500 high-frequency words to make Complete the Words and Listen and Repeat tractable at A2

cons.claim: Lexical-size figures are population research, not an ETS requirement, so they guide but do not guarantee a band
cons.example: reaching a 3,500-word size yet still missing band 4 because processing speed, not size, is the gap

failure_modes: chasing the ~8-9k academic word-family ceiling before it is needed for the target band
quoting a study-hours-per-band figure the research file marks UNKNOWN
acceptance_tests: the node carries the Milton & Alexiou A2/B1/B2 anchors as FACT, feeds them into R1 and S1, and flags the ~8-9k figure estimate and not required for band 4
revisit_triggers: a newer lexical-size study revises the anchors
the learner's target band changes the needed vocabulary size
an ETS vocabulary guideline appears

nodes.definition: Map Reading task R1, Complete the Words: a ~70-100 word paragraph in which 10 words have their second half deleted and must be typed in, with the first sentence left intact for context [FACT for mechanics, blueprint-derived third parties consistent]. The measured skill is vocabulary knowledge plus orthographic/lexical processing — form-focused reading where the learner must recognise the word from context and reproduce its spelling, not merely understand meaning. Practice form: context-cued word-completion drills (e.g., the free goarno.io 'Complete the Words' drills named in the research file) plus high-frequency spelling practice, using the intact first sentence to seed the topic. It reaches down to A1 difficulty, so it is one of the earliest tasks a from-zero learner can attempt.

included: the ~70-100 word / 10-deleted-second-halves / intact-first-sentence mechanics
vocabulary + orthographic/lexical processing as the skill
the context-cued completion drill and its A1 reachability

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a mechanics change or a spelling-vs-meaning error pattern updates the mapping

pros.claim: A form-completion drill builds exactly the spell-from-context skill this task scores, which pure meaning practice misses
pros.example: drilling second-half completion of high-frequency words seeded by a context sentence

cons.claim: The task rewards spelling/orthography a comprehension-strong learner may neglect, and item-count-per-module varies with the adaptive module
cons.example: a learner who understands the paragraph but mis-types the missing letters and loses the point

failure_modes: practising it as meaning comprehension and ignoring the exact spelling/typing
skipping the intact first sentence that supplies the topic context
acceptance_tests: the mapping states the paragraph/deleted-halves/intact-sentence mechanics, names vocabulary + orthographic/lexical processing, and gives a context-cued completion drill with the A1 reachability noted
revisit_triggers: ETS changes the deletion count or paragraph length
a spelling-vs-meaning error pattern appears in practice
the vocabulary base target changes

nodes.definition: Map Reading task R2, Read in Daily Life: short practical texts (~15-150 words) — emails, texts, menus, bills, announcements — with multiple-choice questions [FACT for mechanics]. The measured skill is comprehension of everyday functional English across an A1-C2 range: locating the asked-for fact, the sender's intent, a time/price/instruction, in a real-world text. Practice form: scan-a-practical-text-for-the-asked-fact drills across the named genres (menus, bills, service announcements), building the habit of reading for the specific functional detail a question targets rather than gist. This is core A2-B1 territory and a natural second step after the A1 form tasks.

included: the ~15-150 word practical-genre texts with MC
everyday functional comprehension as the skill
the scan-for-the-asked-fact drill and its A2-B1 placement

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a genre-set change or a genre-specific weakness updates the mapping

pros.claim: Drilling real-world genres builds the exact functional-reading habit this task scores
pros.example: practising fact-location in menus, bills and announcements rather than gist-reading essays

cons.claim: The genre range is broad and item difficulty spans A1-C2, so a fixed practice level under- or over-shoots parts of it
cons.example: practising only simple menus and being surprised by a denser B2 announcement item

failure_modes: practising gist-reading instead of targeted fact-location
narrowing practice to one genre and missing others in the spread
acceptance_tests: the mapping states the ~15-150 word practical genres with MC, names everyday functional comprehension, and gives a scan-for-the-asked-fact drill with the A2-B1 placement
revisit_triggers: ETS revises the genre set or length band

nodes.definition: Map Reading task R3, Read an Academic Passage: a ~200-word academic passage (down from ~700 words legacy) drawn from history, sciences, social sciences or humanities, followed by ~5 multiple-choice questions, with no prior subject knowledge needed [FACT for mechanics]. The measured skill is academic reading for main idea, supporting detail, inference and vocabulary-in-context. Practice form: short-passage question-type drills that rotate the main-idea / detail / inference / vocab-in-context question families on ~200-word texts, deliberately trained on the shorter 2026 length rather than the ~700-word legacy passage so pacing matches the current form. It sits at the B2-C1 end and, in the upper adaptive module, reaches C1/C2.

included: the ~200-word passage (vs ~700 legacy) + ~5 MC, no-prior-knowledge
main-idea/detail/inference/vocab-in-context as the skill
the short-passage question-family drill and its B2-C1/C2 reach

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a passage-length or question-count change updates the mapping

pros.claim: Training on the shorter 2026 passage length matches real pacing better than legacy 700-word practice
pros.example: rotating question families on ~200-word texts so the learner is not over-trained on long-passage stamina

cons.claim: Most legacy prep still uses ~700-word passages, so easily available material mis-sets the length and pacing

failure_modes: practising on legacy 700-word passages and mis-calibrating pacing

acceptance_tests: the mapping states the ~200-word (vs ~700 legacy) + ~5 MC form, names main-idea/detail/inference/vocab-in-context, and gives a short-passage question-family drill with the B2-C1/C2 reach
revisit_triggers: ETS revises the passage length or question count

nodes.definition: Map Listening task L1, Listen and Choose a Response: about 8 short items where the learner hears a single spoken line and picks the appropriate reply [FACT for the type enumeration; ~8 count and per-type counts vary by adaptive module, ESTIMATE]. The measured skill is interactional listening / pragmatic response selection — recognising the function of an utterance (a request, offer, complaint, invitation) and the socially appropriate reply. Practice form: hear-a-line-pick-the-reply drills that pair spoken prompts with candidate responses, training function recognition and register-appropriate reactions rather than content recall. It is a discrete, quick-item skill distinct from the longer L2-L4 passage tasks.

included: the ~8 short hear-a-line / pick-a-reply items
pragmatic response selection as the skill
the function-recognition reply drill
excluded: the exact per-module item count (adaptive, estimate)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an item-type change or a confirmed module count updates the mapping

pros.claim: Drilling function recognition builds the pragmatic-reply skill this task uniquely scores
pros.example: practising picking the appropriate reply to a request vs a complaint rather than recalling facts

cons.claim: The item count and exact format are adaptive-module dependent and third-party reported, so specifics are estimates
cons.example: assuming exactly 8 items when the count varies by module

failure_modes: practising it as content recall instead of pragmatic reply selection
treating the ~8-item count as a fixed ETS number
acceptance_tests: the mapping states the short hear-a-line / pick-a-reply items, names pragmatic response selection, gives a function-recognition drill, and tags the item count estimate
revisit_triggers: ETS revises the item type or count
a register/function-recognition weakness appears
adaptive module counts are confirmed

nodes.definition: Map Listening task L2, Daily Life Conversation: a two-person dialogue (~90 seconds) followed by ~5 questions [FACT for the type; timing/count blueprint-derived]. The measured skill is conversation comprehension — tracking the main point, distinguishing facts from opinions, catching agreement/disagreement and verbal cues (tone, hesitation, emphasis) between two speakers. Practice form: dialogue-comprehension drills that ask, after a ~90-second two-speaker clip, for the main point, a fact-vs-opinion split and who agrees with what, training the learner to hold two viewpoints at once. It is everyday A2-B1 functional listening, the aural twin of Read in Daily Life.

included: the ~90s two-person dialogue + ~5 questions
main-point / facts-vs-opinions / agreement / verbal-cue comprehension
the two-viewpoint dialogue drill and its A2-B1 placement
excluded: the single-speaker announcement (L3) and academic talk (L4)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a dialogue-format change or a fact-vs-opinion weakness updates the mapping

pros.claim: Drilling fact-vs-opinion and agreement in two-speaker clips builds exactly what this task scores
pros.example: identifying which speaker gives an opinion and where they disagree after a ~90-second dialogue

cons.claim: The ~90s length and ~5-question count are blueprint estimates that can vary by module
cons.example: assuming a fixed 5 questions when the adaptive module changes the count

failure_modes: listening only for facts and missing the opinion/agreement layer
treating the timing/count as ETS-fixed
acceptance_tests: the mapping states the ~90s two-person dialogue + ~5 questions, names main-point/facts-vs-opinions/agreement/verbal-cue comprehension, and gives a two-viewpoint dialogue drill at A2-B1
revisit_triggers: ETS revises the dialogue length or question count
a fact-vs-opinion weakness appears

nodes.definition: Map Listening task L3, Daily Life Announcement: a short single-speaker announcement (~90 seconds) followed by ~5 questions [FACT for the type; timing/count blueprint-derived]. The measured skill is extracting key information from public/service speech — a schedule change, a gate/room, a deadline, an instruction — from a one-way monologue with no interlocutor to cross-check. Practice form: announcement-note-taking drills that play a ~90-second public-service clip and ask for the specific key facts (what, when, where, what to do), training rapid key-info capture. It is everyday A2-B1 functional listening, distinct from the two-speaker conversation by its monologue, key-fact-extraction focus.

included: the ~90s single-speaker announcement + ~5 questions
key-information extraction from public/service speech as the skill
the key-fact note-taking drill and its A2-B1 placement

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an announcement-format change or a key-fact weakness updates the mapping

pros.claim: Note-taking drills on public-service clips build the rapid key-fact capture this task scores
pros.example: capturing the changed gate, time and instruction from a ~90-second announcement

cons.claim: The monologue gives no second speaker to cross-check, so a single mis-heard fact carries, and the timing/count are estimates
cons.example: mis-hearing one deadline in a dense announcement with no dialogue to recover it

failure_modes: confusing it with the two-speaker conversation skill
listening for gist and missing the specific key facts questioned
acceptance_tests: the mapping states the ~90s single-speaker announcement + ~5 questions, names key-information extraction, and gives a key-fact note-taking drill at A2-B1
revisit_triggers: ETS revises the announcement length or count
a key-fact-capture weakness appears
the CEFR placement is revised

nodes.definition: Map Listening task L4, Academic Talk: a short lecture-style talk (~90 seconds) followed by ~5 questions [FACT for the type; timing/count blueprint-derived]. The measured skill is academic listening — main idea, supporting detail and speaker purpose/attitude in a single-speaker lecture, the aural counterpart of the academic reading passage. Practice form: short-lecture drills that play a ~90-second academic clip and rotate main-idea / detail / speaker-purpose questions, deliberately using the shorter 2026 talk length rather than the multi-minute legacy lectures so pacing matches. It reaches into B2-C1/C2 in the upper adaptive module and is the hardest of the four listening types for a from-zero learner.

included: the ~90s single-speaker academic talk + ~5 questions
main-idea/detail/speaker-purpose academic listening as the skill
the short-lecture question-rotation drill and its B2-C1/C2 reach

cons.claim: Legacy prep uses long lectures, so common material mis-sets the length, and difficulty reaches C1/C2 in the upper module

failure_modes: practising on long legacy lectures and mis-calibrating pacing

acceptance_tests: the mapping states the ~90s academic talk + ~5 questions, names main-idea/detail/speaker-purpose academic listening, and gives a short-lecture question-rotation drill with the B2-C1/C2 reach
revisit_triggers: ETS revises the talk length or count

nodes.definition: Map Speaking task S1, Listen and Repeat: 7 sentences about campus/daily-life topics, each heard once and repeated aloud [FACT for mechanics]. The measured skill is phonological and oral fluency — intelligibility, rhythm and exact repetition accuracy; the 2026 Speaking scoring guide reportedly includes a descriptor like 'the response exactly repeats the prompt' [FACT that the guide exists; the precise descriptor wording is an ESTIMATE from myspeakingscore.com/search excerpts]. Practice form: hear-once-then-repeat drills on short campus/daily-life sentences, recording and checking word-for-word accuracy and clear pronunciation, and pairing with phonics because the task reaches down to A1. It is a low-floor entry task and shares its phonological base with the vocabulary foundation.

included: the 7-sentence hear-once-repeat-aloud mechanics
phonological/oral fluency, intelligibility and exact repetition accuracy as the skill
the record-and-check repeat drill and its A1 floor

cons.claim: The precise 2026 rubric wording is an estimate, so a learner should not over-optimise a descriptor that is not ETS-confirmed

chasing an unconfirmed rubric descriptor as if ETS-verified
acceptance_tests: the mapping states the 7-sentence hear-once-repeat mechanics, names phonological fluency/intelligibility/exact-repetition-accuracy, gives a record-and-check drill, and tags the rubric-descriptor wording as an estimate

nodes.definition: Map Speaking task S2, Take an Interview: a simulated interview with a prerecorded interviewer, 4 questions on one topic at 45 seconds each with no prep time, questions escalating from personal experience to broader opinion [FACT for mechanics]. The measured skill is spontaneous speech — language use, organization, fluency and coherence produced on the spot without planning. Practice form: no-prep 45-second answer drills where a prompt escalates from a personal question to an opinion question on the same topic, recorded and reviewed for fluency, structure and on-topic development. Because there is no prep time, memorised templates fail; the drill trains rapid on-topic structuring instead. It reaches into B1-C1 and is the harder of the two Speaking tasks.

spontaneous language use/organization/fluency/coherence as the skill

nodes.definition: Map Writing task W1, Build a Sentence: a syntax drill in which the learner assembles or completes sentences [FACT for the type; exact interface detail blueprint-derived and thin in public sources]. The measured skill is grammatical accuracy, word order and syntax control at the sentence level — the discrete-point writing skill under the two longer composition tasks. Practice form: sentence-assembly / word-ordering drills that rebuild scrambled or partial sentences into grammatical ones, isolating syntax from content so errors in agreement, order and structure are trained directly. It reaches down toward A2 and is a low-floor writing entry, feeding the sentence quality the Email and Discussion tasks depend on.

nodes.definition: Map Writing task W2, Write an Email: a 7-minute task to write an email for a given scenario [FACT for mechanics]. The measured skill is practical written communication — register, tone and social/discourse conventions appropriate to the recipient and purpose (a request, apology, enquiry). Practice form: timed 7-minute scenario-email drills across common purposes, checking that greeting, purpose statement, body and sign-off match the register the scenario demands, so the learner writes to the reader rather than in a generic essay voice. It is everyday A2-B1 functional writing, the productive twin of the daily-life reading/listening tasks, and register mismatch is its signature failure.

included: the 7-minute scenario-email mechanics
practical written communication, register and social/discourse conventions as the skill
the timed scenario-email drill and its A2-B1 placement

pros.example: writing a 7-minute apology email vs a request email and matching each register

cons.claim: A learner trained on formal academic essays tends to over-formalise the email and mismatch register
cons.example: writing a casual-scenario email in stiff academic prose and losing register points

failure_modes: writing the email in a generic academic register regardless of scenario
over-running the 7-minute budget with essay-length prose
acceptance_tests: the mapping states the 7-minute scenario-email mechanics, names practical communication/register/conventions, and gives a timed scenario-email drill at A2-B1
revisit_triggers: ETS revises the email time or scenario style

nodes.definition: Map Writing task W3, Writing for an Academic Discussion (WAD): a 10-minute task in which the learner reads a professor's discussion-board prompt plus classmate posts and writes their own reasoned contribution [FACT; the task is carried over from the July 2023 legacy format into 2026, with the ~10-minute timing confirmed by 2026 sources]. The measured skill is reasoned written argument — relevance to the prompt, elaboration of a position, syntactic variety and vocabulary under time pressure. Practice form: timed 10-minute discussion-post drills that read a prompt plus two peer posts and write an on-topic, elaborated contribution, checking that it engages the specific discussion rather than delivering a generic essay. It reaches B2-C1 and is the most demanding writing task for a from-zero learner.

reasoned argument, relevance, elaboration, syntax and vocabulary as the skill

nodes.definition: Set the method for designing the practice-form half of every mapping so a drill is genuinely repeatable and skill-targeted, not a single mock question. A good practice form (1) isolates the one measured skill, (2) matches the current 2026 mechanics (length, timing, no-prep where applicable) rather than legacy dimensions, (3) is repeatable with fresh content, and (4) has a self-check the learner can score. It is anchored on the free official spine — ETS TestReady's daily rotating activity and the free January-2026 sample/familiarisation test — with third-party drills (e.g., goarno.io Complete the Words) layered on and their unaudited quality flagged [FACT that these free resources exist; third-party item quality UNKNOWN]. This node standardises how R2, L2, W1 and every other type turn into a drill.

nodes.definition: Align practice for the productive Speaking and Writing tasks to the scoring rubrics without over-claiming. Legacy ETS rubrics are published: Speaking on General Description, Delivery, Language Use and Topic Development, and Writing on relevant, clearly expressed contribution with syntactic variety, vocabulary and few errors [FACT that these dimensions exist]. For 2026, new ETS Speaking and Writing scoring guides exist [FACT existence], and third-party/search-excerpt reporting says Listen and Repeat is scored on fluency, intelligibility and repeat accuracy, Take an Interview adds language use and organization, and Writing tasks on elaboration/relevance, syntax/vocabulary and social/discourse conventions [ESTIMATE - medium]. The exact 2026 dimension weightings are an UNKNOWN blocker (the ETS rubric PDFs were not fetchable) and must not be quoted as fact. nodes.definition: Map the underlying skills that serve more than one task so study time compounds. High-frequency vocabulary and phonics sit under both Complete the Words (R1) and Listen and Repeat (S1); everyday functional comprehension sits under Read in Daily Life (R2), Daily Life Conversation (L2) and Daily Life Announcement (L3); short-passage academic processing links Read an Academic Passage (R3) and Academic Talk (L4); sentence-level syntax from Build a Sentence (W1) underlies both the Email (W2) and the Discussion post (W3). The transfer map tells a from-zero learner which single drill pays off across tasks, and which skills are genuinely task-specific (exact repetition for S1; register for W2; no-prep spontaneity for S2) and cannot be borrowed from a neighbour.

nodes.definition: Map the retired legacy 2023-2025 task types onto the current skills so a learner can still mine legacy prep without mistaking it for the live line-up. Legacy Speaking had 4 tasks (Task 1 Independent opinion with 15s prep/45s speak; Tasks 2-4 Integrated read/listen/speak with 30s prep/60s speak) — its spontaneous-opinion skill maps onto Take an Interview, though the 2026 task removes prep time [ESTIMATE - high confidence, standard published description]. Legacy Reading used two ~700-word passages / 20 questions and legacy Listening 28 questions — their academic reading/listening skills map onto the shorter 2026 academic passage and talk. Legacy Writing paired an Integrated task (retired) with Writing for an Academic Discussion, which alone carries straight into 2026. The rule: reuse legacy material for the underlying skill, re-time and re-length it to current mechanics, and drop tasks (Independent Speaking, Integrated Writing/Speaking, long passages) that no longer exist.

nodes.definition: Compose the deliverable the KB builds toward: the full section-skills syllabus as a table of every 2026 question type -> underlying skill -> practice form, sequenced by the CEFR ladder and cross-linked by the skill-transfer map, with legacy tasks mapped alongside and productive-task practice aligned to the (estimated) rubrics. The syllabus orders a from-zero learner: build vocabulary/phonics under the A1 form tasks (R1, S1), then the everyday functional cluster (R2, L2, L3, W2), then the academic tasks (R3, L4, W3) and the no-prep interview (S2), scoring each against a self-check. It carries the honesty envelope end to end: item counts and rubric dimensions are estimates, and the exact on-test SECTION ORDER is an UNKNOWN blocker (sources conflict — some report Reading-Listening-Speaking-Writing, one reports Reading-Listening-Writing-Speaking; ETS content page unreachable), so the syllabus does not prescribe an order-dependent test-day strategy.

conflict_axes.name: form_focused_vs_meaning_focused_reading
conflict_axes.description: Complete the Words rewards form/orthography while the academic passage rewards meaning/inference, so early reading study is pulled between spelling-from-context and comprehension.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: sequence by CEFR: form-completion and vocabulary first at A1, meaning-focused academic reading up as the learner reaches B2

conflict_axes.name: mimicry_accuracy_vs_spontaneous_production
conflict_axes.description: Listen and Repeat rewards exact mimicry while Take an Interview rewards unplanned spontaneous speech, two opposing oral skills competing for Speaking practice time.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use Listen and Repeat as the A1 phonological entry and add no-prep spontaneity drills for the interview only once intelligibility is stable

conflict_axes.name: legacy_prep_material_vs_current_format
conflict_axes.description: Abundant legacy prep describes retired tasks, tempting practice on the wrong line-up versus the scarcer current-format material.
poles: use the plentiful legacy material as-is
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: reuse legacy material only for the underlying skill, re-timed and re-lengthened to 2026 mechanics, and drop retired tasks

conflict_axes.name: vocab_breadth_vs_academic_depth
conflict_axes.description: A beginner can chase the ~8-9k academic word-family ceiling or consolidate the ~2-3.5k high-frequency base the easiest tasks actually need.
poles: push toward the academic word-family ceiling
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: target the Milton & Alexiou A2-B2 high-frequency base for band 4 and defer the ~8-9k academic ceiling, which is not required for band 4

conflict_axes.name: syntax_drill_vs_extended_argument
conflict_axes.description: Build a Sentence isolates syntax while the discussion post demands extended reasoning, so writing practice is split between micro-accuracy and macro-argument.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: build sentence-level accuracy first as the foundation, then layer timed extended-argument practice for the email and discussion post

conflict_axes.name: speed_under_adaptive_vs_accuracy
conflict_axes.description: The two-stage adaptive Reading/Listening rewards sustaining accuracy into harder Stage 2 items, pitting pace against precision.
poles: prioritise speed to reach more items
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: practise ramped timed sets that hold accuracy into a harder Stage 2 rather than optimising raw speed or untimed precision alone

conflict_axes.name: daily_life_register_vs_academic_register
conflict_axes.description: Everyday tasks (Read in Daily Life, Write an Email) reward casual/functional register while academic tasks reward formal register, and mixing them costs points.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: practise register-matching to the scenario: functional for daily-life tasks, formal for academic ones, and never default the email to academic prose

conflict_axes.name: official_spec_fidelity_vs_third_party_estimate
conflict_axes.description: The ETS Blueprint and rubric PDFs were unreachable, so precise counts/dimensions exist only as third-party estimates that tempt over-precise planning.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: carry item counts and rubric dimensions as tagged estimates, plan on ranges, and revise against ETS when its pages become reachable

conflict_axes.name: rubric_targeted_practice_vs_authentic_task_practice
conflict_axes.description: Practising to isolated rubric dimensions can drift from authentic whole-task performance, especially when the exact 2026 weightings are unknown.
poles: drill each rubric dimension in isolation
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: score authentic whole-task responses against the dimension checklist and target the weakest dimension, rather than drilling dimensions divorced from the task

edge_cases.mitigation: use the era split to confirm 2026 Speaking is Listen and Repeat + Take an Interview and map only the legacy spontaneous-opinion skill forward

edge_cases.description: A test-day strategy is built on a fixed section order that the sources do not agree on
edge_cases.trigger: an order-dependent plan assumes Reading-Listening-Speaking-Writing as certain
edge_cases.mitigation: treat the on-test section order as an UNKNOWN blocker, avoid order-dependent strategy, and confirm against the ETS content page when reachable

edge_cases.description: Third-party blueprint item counts are quoted to a learner as the official ETS specification
edge_cases.trigger: a '50 Reading items, 35 points' figure is presented as ETS-confirmed
edge_cases.mitigation: tag the counts as triangulated third-party estimates and revise against the ETS Blueprint PDF when fetchable

edge_cases.description: Complete the Words is practised as pure meaning comprehension, ignoring exact spelling of the deleted second halves
edge_cases.trigger: the learner understands the paragraph but mistypes the missing letters
edge_cases.mitigation: drill context-cued form completion with word-for-word spelling checks, using the intact first sentence for topic context

edge_cases.description: Listen and Repeat is practised as paraphrase rather than exact repetition
edge_cases.trigger: the learner restates the sentence in their own words instead of repeating it
edge_cases.mitigation: record hear-once-repeat attempts and check word-for-word accuracy and intelligibility against the prompt

edge_cases.description: The learner memorises templates for Take an Interview despite its no-prep, escalating questions
edge_cases.trigger: a prep-time legacy strategy is applied to the no-prep 2026 interview
edge_cases.mitigation: practise no-prep 45-second answers on escalating personal-to-opinion prompts to build spontaneous structuring, not templates

edge_cases.description: The scenario email is written in stiff academic prose, mismatching the required functional register
edge_cases.trigger: a learner trained on academic essays over-formalises a casual email scenario
edge_cases.mitigation: drill register-matching across email purposes so greeting, body and sign-off fit the scenario's register

edge_cases.description: The Academic Discussion post is a generic essay that ignores the specific professor prompt and peer posts
edge_cases.trigger: a memorised opinion is delivered instead of engaging the thread
edge_cases.mitigation: practise timed 10-minute posts that explicitly reference the prompt and at least one peer point to hold relevance

edge_cases.description: An estimated 2026 rubric dimension or weighting is quoted to a learner as ETS-confirmed
edge_cases.trigger: a search-excerpt rubric summary is treated as the fetched ETS rubric PDF
edge_cases.mitigation: flag the exact 2026 rubric weightings as an UNKNOWN blocker, use only the estimated dimension checklist, and revise when the ETS rubric PDFs are fetchable

edge_cases.description: A beginner chases the ~8-9k academic word-family ceiling not required for a band-4 target
edge_cases.trigger: the academic vocabulary figure is treated as a prerequisite for the everyday tasks
edge_cases.mitigation: consolidate the Milton & Alexiou A2-B2 high-frequency base for band 4 and defer the academic ceiling until targeting C1

edge_cases.description: Build a Sentence is practised as free writing, losing the isolated-syntax focus the task scores
edge_cases.trigger: the sentence-assembly constraint is dropped for open composition
edge_cases.mitigation: keep the drill on reordering/completing given sentences to isolate agreement, word order and structure

edge_cases.description: Academic reading/listening is practised on legacy ~700-word passages and multi-minute lectures, mis-calibrating pacing to the shorter 2026 forms
edge_cases.trigger: legacy-length material is used without re-lengthening to the ~200-word passage and ~90-second talk
edge_cases.mitigation: rebuild academic drills to the 2026 ~200-word passage and ~90-second talk lengths so pacing matches

workflow.action: Establish the type -> skill -> practice-form mapping method
workflow.description: Decompose each question type into the measured skill and a drillable form as the unit of work
workflow.gate: the type -> skill -> form triple is stated with one worked example

workflow.action: Fix the current-2026 vs legacy era boundary
workflow.description: Date the Jan 21 2026 overhaul, list headline changes, and the legacy line-up, with the ETS-unreachable caveat
workflow.gate: the overhaul and legacy line-ups are stated with the search-excerpt honesty caveat

workflow.action: Model the two-stage adaptive Reading/Listening structure
workflow.description: State the same-Stage-1 / adjusting-Stage-2 mechanic and the added pacing skill, tagging counts as estimates
workflow.gate: the mechanic and pacing skill are stated and item counts are tagged third-party estimates

workflow.action: Place the tasks on the CEFR ladder and anchor the vocabulary base
workflow.description: Spread the tasks A1-C2, prescribe functional-before-academic order, and carry the Milton & Alexiou anchors
workflow.gate: each task is placed on the ladder and the FACT vocabulary anchors are carried with the academic ceiling flagged estimate

workflow.action: Map the three Reading question types
workflow.description: Map Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life and Read an Academic Passage to skill and drill
workflow.gate: each Reading type names its 2026 mechanics, skill and a current-length drill

workflow.action: Map the four Listening question types
workflow.description: Map Listen and Choose a Response, Daily Life Conversation, Daily Life Announcement and Academic Talk
workflow.gate: each Listening type names its skill and drill and flags per-type counts as adaptive estimates

workflow.description: Map Listen and Repeat (exact repetition) and Take an Interview (no-prep spontaneity) to skill and drill
workflow.gate: both Speaking tasks name their mechanics, skill and drill, with the no-prep and exact-repetition conditions stated

workflow.description: Map Build a Sentence, Write an Email and Writing for an Academic Discussion to skill and drill
workflow.gate: each Writing task names its mechanics, skill and drill with the WAD carry-over noted

workflow.action: Standardise the practice-form design per type
workflow.description: Apply the four practice-form criteria and current-mechanics rule, anchored on the free ETS spine
workflow.gate: the four criteria and current-mechanics rule are stated with third-party quality flagged UNKNOWN

workflow.action: Align productive-task practice to the rubrics
workflow.description: Score Speaking/Writing responses against the dimension checklist, targeting the weakest dimension
workflow.gate: legacy dimensions are FACT, 2026 dimensions are estimates, and exact weightings are flagged UNKNOWN

workflow.action: Map shared skills and compose the full syllabus
workflow.description: Draw the skill-transfer links, map legacy tasks alongside, and compose the CEFR-sequenced type -> skill -> form table
workflow.gate: the syllabus composes the table, states the from-zero order, carries the estimate tags, and flags section order UNKNOWN with no order-dependent strategy

priority_rationale: The mapping frame, format era split, adaptive model, CEFR ladder and vocabulary foundation come first because every question-type mapping depends on knowing the era, the adaptive structure, the difficulty level and the vocabulary base a task sits on; the per-section task nodes (Reading, Listening, Speaking, Writing) next instantiate the frame for each 2026 type with its skill and drill; the cross-cutting practice-form design, rubric alignment, skill-transfer map and legacy map then turn the mappings into repeatable, rubric-aware, transfer-linked, legacy-safe drills; and the composed section-skills syllabus comes last because it sequences every upstream mapping up the CEFR ladder into one from-zero study path with the estimate/UNKNOWN honesty envelope carried end to end.

dominance_rules.rule: The current-2026 format dominates any legacy task description
dominance_rules.rationale: legacy prep is abundant but describes retired tasks that are no longer on the test
dominance_rules.trigger: a task list is taken from a resource of uncertain era
dominance_rules.action: verify the task against the Jan 21 2026 line-up and drop any legacy-only task before drilling it

dominance_rules.rule: The measured skill dominates the surface format as the study target
dominance_rules.rationale: ETS can revise the interface but the underlying language skill persists and transfers
dominance_rules.trigger: study is being planned around a task name
dominance_rules.action: map the task to its underlying skill and drill the skill, adding only the minimum format-specific rehearsal

dominance_rules.rule: A tagged estimate dominates a convenient precise number
dominance_rules.rationale: the ETS Blueprint and rubric PDFs were unreachable, so precise counts/dimensions are third-party estimates only
dominance_rules.trigger: an exact item count, timing or rubric weighting is about to be stated as fact
dominance_rules.action: carry it as a tagged estimate/range and mark exact rubric weightings and section order UNKNOWN, revising against ETS when reachable

dominance_rules.rule: The CEFR ladder dominates the raw task list for sequencing a beginner
dominance_rules.rationale: a from-zero learner must build reachable A1-B1 tasks before the academic ceiling
dominance_rules.trigger: a beginner starts on the academic passage or interview first
dominance_rules.action: sequence practice up the CEFR ladder from the A1 form/repeat tasks through the functional cluster to the academic tasks

dominance_rules.rule: Exact-repetition and no-prep-spontaneity are treated as distinct, non-substitutable skills
dominance_rules.rationale: Listen and Repeat mimicry and Take an Interview spontaneity are opposing oral skills
dominance_rules.trigger: one Speaking drill is used to cover both tasks
dominance_rules.action: drill exact repetition and no-prep spontaneity separately and do not substitute one for the other

dominance_rules.rule: Register-matching dominates a default writing voice
dominance_rules.rationale: the email rewards functional register and the discussion post formal register, and mismatch costs points
dominance_rules.trigger: an email or post is written in a single default register
dominance_rules.action: match register to the scenario, functional for the email and formal for the academic post

dominance_rules.rule: Current-length academic drills dominate legacy-length practice
dominance_rules.rationale: the 2026 passage (~200 words) and talk (~90 seconds) are far shorter than the legacy forms, changing pacing
dominance_rules.trigger: academic practice uses legacy ~700-word passages or multi-minute lectures
dominance_rules.action: rebuild academic drills to the 2026 lengths so pacing matches the real test

dominance_rules.rule: The high-frequency vocabulary base dominates the academic word-family ceiling for band-4 targets
dominance_rules.rationale: the ~8-9k academic ceiling is an estimate not required for band 4, while the A2-B2 base is the FACT anchor
dominance_rules.trigger: a beginner chases the academic vocabulary ceiling
dominance_rules.action: consolidate the Milton & Alexiou A2-B2 high-frequency base first and defer the academic ceiling to C1 targets

anti_rework_rules.rule: Confirm a resource's format era before drilling any task from it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: hours spent drilling retired legacy tasks (Independent Speaking, Integrated Writing, long passages) that are not on the 2026 test

anti_rework_rules.rule: Map each task to its underlying skill before building a drill
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a format-specific rehearsal that must be rebuilt when ETS revises the interface

anti_rework_rules.rule: Tag every item count, timing and rubric dimension as estimate/UNKNOWN when first written
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a precise-looking plan being retracted when the ETS blueprint or rubric PDFs are finally read

anti_rework_rules.rule: Build academic reading/listening drills to the 2026 ~200-word / ~90-second lengths from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: pacing mis-calibrated on legacy 700-word passages and long lectures that must be redone

anti_rework_rules.rule: Practise Take an Interview with no prep time from the start
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a memorised-template habit that fails on the real no-prep task and has to be unlearned

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the email and discussion drills to their real 7- and 10-minute budgets when practice begins
anti_rework_rules.prevents: over-long essay habits that overrun the timed tasks and need re-training

anti_rework_rules.rule: Score productive-task practice against the dimension checklist, not an overall impression
anti_rework_rules.prevents: plateauing on a hidden weakest dimension that a later diagnosis forces a re-plan to fix

anti_rework_rules.rule: Sequence a beginner up the CEFR ladder rather than starting at the academic ceiling
anti_rework_rules.prevents: early demoralising failure on B2+ tasks and a restart at the reachable A1-B1 level

iteration_protocol.trigger: the ETS 2026 Blueprint & Specifications PDF becomes fetchable and confirms or corrects the per-module item counts and timing
iteration_protocol.action: replace the estimated counts/timing in the adaptive model and recompose the syllabus table

iteration_protocol.trigger: the ETS 2026 Speaking/Writing rubric PDFs become fetchable and confirm the exact dimensions and weightings
iteration_protocol.action: replace the estimated rubric dimensions and remove the UNKNOWN-weighting blocker in the rubric alignment

iteration_protocol.trigger: the ETS content page confirms the on-test section order
iteration_protocol.action: resolve the section-order UNKNOWN blocker and add any order-dependent test-day guidance to the syllabus

iteration_protocol.trigger: ETS renames, adds or removes a 2026 question type
iteration_protocol.action: remap the affected type to its skill and drill and update the transfer map and syllabus

iteration_protocol.trigger: the full ETS CEFR-to-band cell table becomes available
iteration_protocol.action: sharpen the CEFR placement of each task and the reachable-first ordering for a beginner

iteration_protocol.trigger: the legacy transition/dual-reporting period ends (~Jan 2028) and legacy material is deprecated
iteration_protocol.action: downgrade the legacy task map to historical reference and drop legacy-only guidance from the syllabus

iteration_protocol.trigger: a third-party practice drill is found mis-calibrated against the official spec
iteration_protocol.action: flag the drill, re-anchor the practice form on the free ETS spine, and note the audit gap

iteration_protocol.trigger: a newer lexical-size study revises the CEFR-to-vocabulary anchors
iteration_protocol.action: update the vocabulary foundation anchors and the beginner ordering that depends on them
